name: Ada
title: Lamech's wife and mother of Jabal and Jubal
summary: Ada is the first of Lamech's two wives mentioned in Cain's genealogy in Genesis 4. Through her sons Jabal and Jubal, she became the matriarch of two important cultural traditions: nomadic livestock herding and musical performance. These contributions place Ada at the center of the emergence of early human civilization as portrayed in the biblical primeval history. At the same time, she stands in a lineage marked by increasing violence and distance from God, which Lamech's song of violence to her and Zillah dramatically illustrates. Lamech's marriage to Ada and Zillah also marks the Bible's first explicit mention of polygamy, underscoring the gradual moral decline in the generations after Cain.
roles: matriarch of nomadic herdsmen and musicians

keyEvents.title: Mentioned as Lamech's wife
keyEvents.description: Ada is mentioned as one of Lamech's two wives, making him the first person in the Bible to explicitly practice polygamy.

keyEvents.title: Mother of Jabal
keyEvents.description: Ada bore Jabal, who became the ancestor of those who live in tents and keep livestock – the first nomadic shepherds.

keyEvents.title: Mother of Jubal
keyEvents.description: Ada also bore Jubal, who became the ancestor of all who play stringed instruments and wind instruments – the founder of music.

keyEvents.title: Part of Cain's lineage
keyEvents.description: Ada belonged to Cain's lineage, which developed civilization, craftsmanship, and culture, but according to the biblical narrative also moved increasingly further away from God.

keyEvents.title: Lamech's Song of Violence
keyEvents.description: Lamech addressed Ada and Zillah directly in his poetic song about violence and revenge. The song illustrates the escalating violence and moral decay in Cain's line, standing in sharp contrast to God's protection of Cain.

footnotes.text: The name Ada (Hebrew: עָדָה, Adah) likely means 'ornament' or 'jewel', derived from the Hebrew verb עדה ('to adorn' or 'to decorate'). The name also appears later in the Bible as the name of one of Esau's wives (Gen 36:2), showing that the name remained in use through generations.

Lamech's marriage to two wives (Ada and Zillah) constitutes the first explicit example of polygamy in the Bible. Several theologians interpret this as a sign of moral decay in Cain's lineage, in contrast to the monogamous model presented in the creation account (Gen 2:24).

Ada's sons Jabal and Jubal represent the beginning of specialized professions and cultural development. Jabal is linked to nomadic animal husbandry and Jubal to musical instruments. Together with Tubal-Cain (son of Zillah), this testifies to an advanced civilization in Cain's lineage – a development of technology and culture that, according to the biblical narrative, took place alongside increasing distance from God.

Lamech's song (Gen 4:23–24) is considered one of the oldest poetic texts in the Bible. The Hebrew original has a distinct poetic structure with parallelisms and rhythmic construction. Several rabbinic commentators, including those in Bereshit Rabbah, interpret the song as an expression of escalating violence and pride, viewing it as a turning point in humanity's moral development before the Flood.

Archaeological finds from the ancient Middle East confirm that nomadic animal husbandry and early musical performance were among the earliest forms of human cultural specialization. Primitive bone flutes have been found from very early periods, which aligns with the biblical account of Jubal as the father of music.
